Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: FRANS-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And it says: "Sumadin Cesare [phoen] from Prizren made a confession in front of Gak's and Hutsch's running cameras, which must have made the investigation reporters very happy. Cesare was a high-sounding described as 'one of the most influential men in Kosovo', which was, to put it mildly, not a very good assessment of the man still judged as a showoff. Cesare, a former regional commander of the Kosovo Albanian underground army, UCK, was on top of that, or so say Gak and Hutsch, a paid informant of the BND, Bundis Nachtrichter Dins [phoen]." That's the German Secret Services, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: FRANS-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: "The ZDF claims to have found out that Cesare gave the green light to the long-planned riots on Serbian minorities on the phone, in a telephone conversation of March 4th, 2004, which was listened in on by the BND. He used code words like 'hot party' and 'a bold atmosphere'." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: FRANS-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Then I'll ask you to read the next paragraph. It says: "The control collegiums of the German Parliament decided, in the first round of a secret session on November 24th, 2004, that there was nothing that the BND could be blamed for. This was said by the chairman of the secret committee, Hartmut Buttner. The ZDF stays with their description and don't have any doubt in the credibility of their colleague Hutsch. The story got lost in the sand of sensation journalist in the meantime, and that's where it belongs." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: FRANS-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And you recall this original finding of the of the Parliamentary Commission in Germany which basically expressed the view that there was nothing to that; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: FRANS-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that it said that it was November 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Then I'll ask you to turn to the next page, Mr. Hutsch. It says: "In ZDF, Gak and Hutsch caught an alleged 'NATO dossier' from May 17th, 2002, it was not said by whom it was made and for whom, in which it was claimed 'the Islamic' Cesare has made connections to the Lebanese terror group Hezbollah and to the terror network al-Qaeda of Osama Bin Laden, and has kept them up until the beginning of the disturbances. A powerful presentation for a computer, which in principle can be made by anyone." Do you recall Mr. Hutsch, saying that?

utterances.speaker: FRANS-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, it's what I read.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do you recall also relying on a famous NATO dossier?

utterances.speaker: FRANS-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a number of dossiers there, and there was one from the 17th of May, 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do you recall where you received that dossier from?

utterances.speaker: FRANS-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I know where it comes from, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And where does it come from?

utterances.speaker: FRANS-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That you have to ask my colleague, Hans Ulrich Gak and my colleague Jaspas [phoen], because what this article doesn't show is that it was a network project from -- all in all for journalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Okay. We're going to come to that in a bit of time. But are you saying, sir, that you have no idea where this dossier comes from of the 17th of --

utterances.speaker: FRANS-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have an idea, but I wouldn't do everything to open a source from one of my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, can you tell this Chamber where you got that dossier from, sir?

utterances.speaker: FRANS-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that two of my colleagues got this dossier and that it was given to Herb Jaspas and to Mr. Hans Ulrich Gak.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do you know where Mr. Jaspas and Mr. Gak got this document from, sir?

utterances.speaker: FRANS-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat: I won't any source in front of the Chamber that is from my colleagues. You will have to ask my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Perhaps, Your Honour, we'll go into a private session for a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: So if I can ask you to go to the next paragraph of Mr. Rub's article, it says this: "But if Cesare really was connected to Hezbollah and al-Qaeda, why in the world would he reveal this to two German journalists who sold their reports right away to ZDF and the Swiss Boulevard paper "Sonntags Blicke. [phoen]" Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: FRANS-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And then there's a paragraph which relates to you, the next one:

utterances.speaker: MR. RUB SAYS THIS
utterances.text: "Useful information about the free journalist, Frans-Josef Hutsch, born in Aachen in 1963 might be that he was the fourth witness of the Defence in the process against the former Serbian and Yugoslav president, Slobodan Milosevic, at the International War Crimes Tribunal in The Hague on October 12 and 13, 2004". Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: FRANS-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Then he says: "Before he decided career on a career in journalism, Hutsch was a career soldier in the German army for more than 14 years. According to his testimony, he retired with the rank of a major." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: FRANS-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Isn't it the case, sir, that two days ago you told this Chamber and you told the Prosecution that you retired in the rank of captain in the army?

utterances.speaker: FRANS-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And what rank was it that you retired, major or captain?

utterances.speaker: FRANS-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: So this is wrong?

utterances.speaker: FRANS-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if you had told the Trial Chamber in the Milosevic case that you retired as a major, that would also be wrong?

utterances.speaker: FRANS-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was asked which was the next rank that I would get, and after captain the rank of major comes. That's already what I was discussing with the Prosecution in the preparing of today.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: You were not asked what the next rank was, sir. You were asked what the rank was when you left the army. I'll read the transcript to you. This is page 32904 of the Milosevic trial transcript of 12 October 2004. And the question asked by Mr. Kaye was: "Q. When you left the German army, what was your rank that you left at? "A. I left the military as major, and I'm now in reserve." So you said to the Trial Chamber that you left as a major, is that right, to the Milosevic Chamber?

utterances.speaker: FRANS-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's wrong. I was asked in German what would be the next rank, and I asked -- I answered in German that my next rank will be a major.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm very sorry to interrupt, but I think a fact needs to be clarified here. During this witness's testimony during the trial of Slobodan Milosevic, this witness did not testify in English. This witness testified in German, his first language. An interpreter was used then to interpret this witness's words then into English, and then there was further translation, et cetera, et cetera. And that's, I believe, in the record, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, I believe this is a point that the witness should make if he feels he has to do it, not the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Sir, can you say in German what's the word for captain?

utterances.speaker: FRANS-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hauptman.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: That's correct. And for Major, can you tell us what the word for is?

utterances.speaker: FRANS-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: That's right. Thank you very much. If we can turn now to the next paragraph of that statement, but perhaps we'll leave this question of your rank, sir. What rank did you have between September 2001 and November 2001 when you worked as an officer for the army or for the embassy in Macedonia; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: FRANS-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, captain, because all these documents I have here with me, they show that.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: So any suggestion that at the time you were an uber lieutenant or a first lieutenant would be wrong; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANS-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could go back to the transcript or the article of Mr. Rub, still the second page of it, I'd like to read the paragraph that starts with: "Whoever ..." Can you see that? This is 1D002803. It's 1D280. Your Honour, it's under tab 11 of the binder, page 2. Sir, can you see the paragraph starting with the words in English: "Whoever run into the colleague in the Balkans"; can you see that?

utterances.speaker: FRANS-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'll read the paragraph to you: "Whoever run into the colleague in the Balkans," and it's referring to you, "where he reported for papers like the"Hamburger Adendblatt" can most of all remember that Hutsch does not show modesty in his reports of military and secret things. Apparently the man has been so lucky to see and hear everything that the historical actors usually try to hide from the public and from other journalists. Hutsch seems to be flooded with secret information from all war parties, and one was supposed to believe that the sources which gave out the information didn't talk for any other reasons but because the world should finally hear the truth." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: FRANS-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Then Mr. Rub continues: "It should be noted that all the actual or made-up secret information always come to journalists exactly that, when the sources are aiming at something. A reporter should be suspicious when the usually silent people start talking." Then I'll turn your attention to the next paragraph of that article of Mr. Rub. "In the Milosevic process, Hutsch mostly talked about the time between September 1998 and December 1999, in which he reported about the UCK. He said he obtained exact knowledge about the organisation of the UCK, about their war tactics, their weapons, and their supply lines from Albania and Macedonia. The essence of his testimony in The Hague is that the war of the UCK was a made-up war. The UCK seems to have a really good PR adviser. There were situations where refugees were kept in the woods until the Western journalists came. There were situations when civilians in the village were kept throughout the attacks of the Serbian police, the civilians were prevented from to leaving the villages, the UCK have used their people as human protection shields. Do you recall in the Milosevic case, Mr. Hutsch, making the suggestion that the UCK would stage crime scenes and that they a good PR adviser?

utterances.speaker: FRANS-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And then it says this: "Hutsch does not mention the massacre of the families of UCK founders Ahmeti by the Serbian soldiers. They were happening from February to March 1998 in the region Drenica and there was 59 deaths in one and 58 in the other. Maybe because he was not in Kosovo at the time. More likely the Serbian officer had lost a patient for the first time at the Christmas intervention." Then there's another passage which talks about evidence which you describe in relation to the Racak incident, and then there's this which is said by Mr. Rub: "It cannot be surprising that Hutsch became a star in some Serbian media after such testimonies in The Hague. Because of this, he continues with the 'conspiracy theory' which is popular in Serbia and also more and more popular in Germany. The war about Kosovo was just a rehearsal for the attack in Iraq. The invasion of Iraq is exactly the same as the bombing of Yugoslavia to the smallest detail." Do you recall making that statement to a Serbian journalist, Mr. Hutsch, that in effect your view and your position was that the operation by NATO in Kosovo was merely a warmup exercise for the attack on Iraq?

utterances.speaker: FRANS-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the opinion of General Heinz Loquai which was quoted by me in this interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And you agree that's what you told this journalist as your personal view; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANS-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as my personal view, as a quote from Heinz Loquai.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But you indicated to that journalist, isn't that correct, that you believed this position to be correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANS-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's some good reasons to believe that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you. If we turn --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux, I'm sorry, but we have run out of time by --

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- three minutes, and we must now adjourn and resume tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: p.m., to be reconvened on Friday, June 29, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.
